Neonatal Australian blacktip sharks (Carcharhinus tilstoni) emerge from their mothers at a total length of approximately 60 cm [Lb = approximately 60 cm], a size that equips them well for the warm, productive waters of northern Australia. This length at birth is documented from captures of newly born individuals with open umbilical scars, a standard field technique for identifying neonates. The gestation period that produces these neonates is estimated at around 305 days [ab = around 305 days] under the species' typical environmental conditions, with data collected at a water temperature of 27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C] reflecting the average thermal regime of their tropical habitat. This extended intrauterine development is characteristic of carcharhinid sharks and is thought to be linked to the species' placental viviparous reproductive mode, which allows for substantial nutrient transfer to the developing embryo. The consistency of this temperature across multiple life-history events underscores the importance of stable thermal conditions for the species' reproductive success.

Females of this species attain an impressive ultimate total length of 200 cm [Li = 200 cm], a dimension that places them among the larger members of the genus in Australian waters. Comparisons with other carcharhinid sharks indicate that Carcharhinus tilstoni is moderately sized, with a growth trajectory that prioritizes robust body condition over extreme elongation.

This reproductive strategy makes the species particularly vulnerable to fishing pressure, as removal of large mature females can have disproportionate effects on population recruitment.

This trade-off between litter size and offspring quality is evident in the relatively large size of the pups at birth, which enhances their survival prospects in the competitive nursery grounds.
